stories.title: Nearly 900,000 homes lost power on Thanksgiving. Some lost their water too.
stories.dek: A coastal storm with gusts up to 70 mph knocked out power from Virginia to New Jersey. For families on electric well pumps, including ours, no power meant no water.
stories.body:
The turkey was in the oven. Then the lights went out.

A powerful coastal storm tore up the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day, knocking out power to nearly 900,000 homes and businesses by Thursday evening, according to NBC News, citing the tracking site PowerOutage.us.

For millions of families, that meant cold ovens, dark dining rooms and a holiday spent waiting for a repair truck. For some, it meant something worse: no water at all.

How big was it

The number kept climbing all day. Around 10 a.m., about 520,000 customers were in the dark, NBC reported. By early afternoon it was more than 700,000. By about 5:30 p.m., it was nearly 900,000.

As of 4:06 p.m. Eastern, Reuters broke it down by state:

  1. Virginia: more than 174,000
  2. Maryland: more than 172,000
  3. Pennsylvania: almost 170,000
  4. Missouri: more than 117,000
  5. New Jersey: more than 91,000
  6. Delaware: more than 20,000
  7. North Carolina: nearly 16,000

By evening, Pennsylvania had passed Virginia as the hardest-hit state, with more than 215,000 customers out, NBC reported. In the Washington area, more than 160,000 were without power, according to the Capital Weather Gang, as cited by NBC.

A “customer” is a home or business on a power bill, not a person. Each one can be a whole family. So the number of people who spent Thanksgiving without power is likely far higher than 900,000.

What hit them

Wind, mostly. The National Weather Service reported or forecast gusts of 50 to 70 mph across parts of Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, New York and coastal New England, Reuters reported. Gusts topped 60 mph in Delaware, North Carolina, Virginia and West Virginia by late morning, bringing down trees and power lines, NBC reported.

In New York, Central Park gusted to 48 mph around 12:20 p.m. LaGuardia Airport clocked 56 mph in the afternoon.

Rain soaked the ground first, which made it easier for wind to rip trees out by the roots. Utilities had warned about exactly that, Reuters reported.

Water where it shouldn’t be

On the coast, the storm piled ocean water onto already-high “king tides.” Some places saw water levels higher than during Superstorm Sandy in 2012, NBC reported:

  1. Wachapreague, Virginia: 9.94 feet, a foot and a half above its Sandy level
  2. Cape May, New Jersey: 9.41 feet, tying its record
  3. Atlantic City: 8.28 feet, the highest since Sandy

Virginia closed the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel and the James River Bridge. People paddled kayaks down flooded streets in Norfolk. New Jersey declared a state of emergency on Wednesday night, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared one for New York City, Long Island and Westchester.

And no water where you need it

Here is the part most coverage skipped.

More than 43 million Americans, about 15% of the country, get their drinking water from a private well, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. The EPA puts it at more than 23 million households.

Most of those wells use an electric pump. When the power goes out, the pump stops, and so does the water. No faucet. No shower. No flushing the toilet after the first one. No washing the Thanksgiving dishes. The National Environmental Health Association tells well owners to switch to a safe source, like bottled water, for drinking, cooking and bathing during an outage.

That includes America House. Our house runs on a well. When the power went out on Thursday, the water went with it.

For families on wells, a power outage is also a water outage, and it lasts exactly as long as the power does.

There is also a safety issue. Michigan’s state well guidance warns that a well system loses pressure during an outage if faucets are opened, and that pressure is part of what keeps contaminants out. NEHA advises having well water tested at a certified lab after an outage, especially if the well was flooded.

Planes, too

Air travel took a hit on one of the busiest weeks of the year. FlightAware counted 417 U.S. flight cancellations on Thursday and about 1,800 delays by the afternoon, Reuters reported. By evening, delays topped 2,000, NBC reported. Washington-area airports, including Reagan National, BWI and Norfolk, were among the hardest hit. United, Delta, Southwest and American let some travelers rebook for free.

Not just the East Coast

In the Midwest, the same system dropped heavy, wet snow. St. Louis got 7.3 inches, and Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, got 14, NBC reported. The utility Ameren warned that restoring power around St. Louis could take “multiple days.”

In New York City, the storm was strong enough to move the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, the first weather postponement in its history.

What officials said

“There is no destination worth risking your safety,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, NBC reported.

Hochul urged New Yorkers to “stay prepared, stay alert, stay informed and stay vigilant as this storm brings heavy wind gusts and strong rainfall this Thanksgiving.”

No deaths had been reported in the coverage we reviewed as of Thursday evening.

If your power is still out

Officials repeat the same advice every storm, because people get hurt every storm:

  1. Generators go outside only. The CDC says: “Never use a generator or other gasoline-powered engines inside your home.” Not in the garage, not in the basement, not with a window open. Ready.gov says to keep it at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages.
  2. Watch for carbon monoxide. It has no color or smell. Headache, dizziness, nausea and confusion are warning signs. Call 911 or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.
  3. Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven.
  4. Food: a closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours. A full freezer lasts about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.
  5. On a well: use stored or bottled water, and get the water tested if the well flooded.
  6. Stay away from downed lines. Assume every one is live.

What happens next

Winds were expected to ease on Friday, with gusts of 25 to 35 mph, Reuters reported. But wet ground and weakened trees mean more can still come down. Utilities had not given clear restoration times for most of the East Coast as of Thursday evening.

Forward

A Thanksgiving blackout is a reminder of how much of daily life runs through one wire. For families on wells, it is two utilities at once. A few gallons of stored water, a working carbon monoxide detector and a plan for the fridge can turn a ruined holiday into an inconvenience. And if you own a well, it is worth asking: what would it take to keep your pump running when the grid goes down?

Did you lose power, or water, this Thanksgiving? Tell us how long it lasted.

stories.title: Driving anywhere on the East Coast for Thanksgiving? You might not be anymore.
stories.dek: More than 30 states face rain, snow, wind or flooding this week, and the worst of it lands on the busiest travel days. What’s coming, where, and what you can do.
stories.body:
Last week, Sydney said she was excited for a real fall Thanksgiving. The East Coast may have taken that a little too literally.

A storm system is lining up to hit the busiest travel days of the year. More than 30 states face rain, snow, wind or flash flooding this week, Fox Weather reported today, and a coastal storm is expected to affect more than 20 states from Florida to Maine.

If you’re flying, driving or hosting this week, here’s what’s coming, one day at a time.

Today, Tuesday: the West gets it first

The trouble started on the West Coast. Pacific storms and seasonal king tides are bringing road closures and thunderstorm delays, with snow on Interstate 5 and Interstate 80, Fox Weather reported. Heavy rain is expected late today in South Florida, around Miami and Fort Lauderdale.

The San Francisco Bay Area is facing what forecasters called potentially “historic” coastal flooding, with water about 3 feet above ground that’s normally dry and surf of 20 to 30 feet, according to Fox Weather. That should ease by Thursday.

Wednesday: the worst day to travel

If you can only change one thing, change Wednesday. Fox Weather called it the worst day to travel for many places.

A rapidly strengthening storm is expected to bring heavy rain and flooding from Florida up through the Carolinas. Airports in Atlanta, Charlotte and Charleston are the ones to watch, along with Interstate 95 and Interstate 26. Along the coast, gusts could reach 40 to 50 mph.

Central Florida is the place this hurts most. The St. Johns River near Cocoa reached nearly 19 feet on Saturday, more than a foot above its old record, Gov. Ron DeSantis said Monday, FOX 35 Orlando reported. Now a flood watch runs from 1 a.m. Wednesday to 1 a.m. Thursday for Brevard, Indian River, St. Lucie, Martin and Okeechobee counties, with 1 to 2 inches of rain expected and 3 to 4 inches possible in spots, the Orlando Sentinel reported, citing the National Weather Service. On ground that’s already soaked, the Weather Service warned, “any rainfall” will “likely result in additional or worsening flooding.” If your drive goes anywhere near the St. Johns, check road closures before you leave.

It’s also one of the busiest travel days of the year. AccuWeather noted that “the Wednesday before Thanksgiving and the Sunday after are among the busiest.” A big storm on a big travel day means delays stack up fast, even at airports that never see a drop of rain, because planes and crews end up in the wrong places.

Thursday: Thanksgiving on I-95

On Thanksgiving Day, the storm moves north. The corridor from Washington to Boston is in its path, and Fox Weather listed delays as possible at Reagan National, Philadelphia, Newark, JFK, LaGuardia and Boston Logan.

Coastal winds could gust up to 60 mph, and power outages are a concern in the Mid-Atlantic and southeastern New England. About 60 million people from Virginia to New England are under a level 1 of 4 risk of flash flooding on Thursday, Fox Weather reported. That’s the lowest level, but heavy rain on a holiday when everyone is on the road still deserves respect.

Here in the D.C. area, that means a wet, windy Thanksgiving. If you’re hosting, it may be worth charging phones and keeping a flashlight near the kitchen, just in case the power blinks mid-turkey.

The Midwest gets its own version. Rain or snow is possible from Detroit to Chicago, and maybe St. Louis. AccuWeather is forecasting accumulating snow in central Illinois, around St. Louis and in the Quad Cities. Washington and Oregon get rain and mountain snow.

Friday to Sunday: the drive home

Friday brings leftover rain, wind and possible snow in New England, the Great Lakes and the interior Northeast, with an icy start in northern New York and New England, according to AccuWeather. By Saturday, most of the headaches should be gone, though rain is expected across the south-central U.S.

Then the West gets another round. A Pacific storm is forecast to bring heavy rain and mountain snow to Washington, Oregon and northern and central California from Sunday into Monday, right as people head home.

What you can actually do

Forecasts can shift, so check again the night before you leave. A few things that help:

  1. Move earlier if you can. “Travelers with flexible plans may be able to avoid some weather-related delays by adjusting their departure time,” AccuWeather advised. Early flights tend to hold up better because delays build through the day.
  2. Book nonstop when possible. Every connection is another chance to get stuck.
  3. Turn on your airline’s app alerts. Airlines often let you change flights for free when a storm is on the way. Look for a travel waiver on their website.
  4. Driving? Plan around the worst hours. Heavy rain and wind on I-95 and I-26 on Wednesday, and I-95 in the Northeast on Thursday, are the stretches to avoid if you have any choice.
  5. Hosting? Have a backup. If guests get delayed, a later dinner beats a stressed-out one.

Forward

No storm changes what the holiday is about. Whether you make it home Wednesday night or Friday morning, the table will still be there, and so will the leftovers. Pack some patience along with the pie.

At America House, we’re hosting Friendsgiving, and we’ll be watching the rain from the kitchen.

Our question for you: what’s the worst Thanksgiving travel story you’ve ever survived? Tell us in the comments.

stories.title: Someone hacked the CIA. The agency that’s supposed to be the hardest to hack.
stories.dek: Hackers got into an unclassified system the CIA and the nation’s top intelligence office use to track the world. Officials say no secrets were touched. Who did it, and what they took, is still unknown.
stories.body:
The CIA is the agency whose whole job is keeping secrets. Today, we learned that someone got into one of its computer systems.

Hackers breached an unclassified system used by the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, The New York Times first reported Tuesday. The Associated Press confirmed a breach of an unclassified CIA system through a person familiar with it, who said it “did not involve any classified information and the issue has been resolved,” according to the AP story published by SecurityWeek.

An ODNI spokesperson said there had been “no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems,” IBTimes reported, citing Reuters. The CIA declined to comment.

What got hit

The system handles what spies call open source intelligence, or OSINT. That’s the “collection and analysis of publicly available data from sources including the internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers,” the AP explained. Nextgov described it as a system “used to analyze public and commercially available information,” which analysts use to track “foreign governments, military activity and other developments.”

So no, nobody has reported that hackers walked off with the CIA’s top-secret files. But “public” doesn’t mean “harmless.”

“Calling this ‘unclassified’ doesn’t make it harmless, though,” Ben Bernstein of the security firm Huntress told Nextgov. Get into a system like this, he said, and “you get a solid look at U.S. intelligence priorities and blind spots without ever touching a classified file.”

Think of it this way. The news articles and satellite photos might be public. What the CIA chooses to look at, how often, and what it ignores is not. That’s the part a rival would want.

What we don’t know yet

Quite a lot, and it’s worth being clear about it.

  1. Who did it. “It was not clear what specific information was compromised or who was responsible,” the AP reported.
  2. What was taken. IBTimes noted that neither the AP nor the Times established whether the data “had been viewed, copied or removed.”
  3. When it happened. No report has said when the break-in started or when it was found.
  4. How far it spread. The Times reported that information at other agencies may also have been exposed. Nextgov, citing the Times, said the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, which handles satellite imagery, was “concurrently affected.”

Nextgov also reported, citing unnamed sources, that an automated hacking tool called ARTEX, built by a Chinese cybersecurity engineer who goes by “Autumn-27,” is “believed to have been used.” No other outlet has confirmed that, and who built a tool doesn’t tell you who used it. No government has blamed anyone.

A very strange month

Here’s why people are paying attention. This isn’t the first odd thing to happen to the federal government’s computers in November.

  1. Nov. 13: A nationwide FAA ground stop, the AP reported, along with a Microsoft outage on Nov. 12 and 13.
  2. Last week: The NSA’s classified network was down for three days before coming back Friday, Nextgov reported. We covered that here.
  3. Last week: The Agriculture Department took several applications offline after a security incident, disrupting payments to farmers, according to Nextgov.
  4. Saturday: The FBI began investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center, the database police use during traffic stops, Newsweek reported.

Officials have said these aren’t connected. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton went on Sunday TV and blamed the outages on a rush to install software patches, and the administration says they are not “part of a coordinated cyberattack,” the AP reported. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was “zero evidence” linking them, according to Newsweek.

That was before today’s news. “No public account has established a connection” between the CIA breach and the other incidents, IBTimes noted. We aren’t saying there is one. But it’s fair to ask the question, and fair to expect an answer.

Why it matters to you

You may never touch a CIA computer. But the agencies hit this month run things you do touch: the flights you take, the police database checked when you’re pulled over, the payments farmers count on and the intelligence that keeps the country safe.

Every one of these systems is only as strong as the oldest patch and the busiest employee. When outages and hacks pile up in the same month, the public deserves a clear explanation of what happened, what was exposed and what’s being fixed, even if the answer is “it’s a coincidence.”

Forward

What to watch: whether the CIA or ODNI says what was taken and who did it, whether Congress calls for a briefing, and whether investigators find any link between this breach and the other incidents this month. So far, no lawmakers have been quoted on it.

What would help: a public timeline. The agencies don’t have to reveal secrets to tell Americans when a breach started, when it was caught and whether it’s over.

Our question for you: is this a coincidence, or do you think someone is testing America’s defenses? Tell us in the comments.

stories.title: One man. One scandal. One very bad week for your 401(k).
stories.dek: Nvidia fell 23% the week Jensen Huang stepped away, and jumped when he came back today. Why does so much of the economy ride on single people, and why do we watch their faces instead of what they do?
stories.body:
Here’s a number that should make anyone with a retirement account sit up. On Monday morning, about a third of the gain in a typical S&P 500 index fund came from one stock, and that stock was moving because of one person.

24/7 Wall St. did the math. On a $500,000 fund, about $7,900 of a $23,900 early gain came from Nvidia alone, a company that makes up only about 5% of the fund.

The person was Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s board brought him back as CEO this morning, 11 days after he resigned.

The week he was gone

Nvidia closed at $162.85 on Nov. 13, the day after Huang resigned, and at $125.53 on Nov. 20. That’s a 23% drop in one week. The S&P 500 fund that millions of Americans own through their 401(k)s fell 8.6% that same week, its worst week since April 2025.

Not all of that is about Huang. Nvidia had been sliding since early October, and by Friday it was 47.5% below its Oct. 6 record. But that one stock accounted for about 36% of the S&P 500 fund’s entire drop over that stretch, 24/7 Wall St. found. If you had $1 million in the fund on Oct. 6, about $41,000 of what you lost came from Nvidia.

Then this morning, one board vote, and it all went the other way.

Nvidia warned us

None of this should surprise Nvidia. In its annual report filed in February, in the section on risks investors should know about, the company wrote, “we are highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team.” It warned that failing to plan for succession “could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success.”

Analyst Dan Ives had put a number on it. Nvidia could lose as much as 30% of its value without Huang, he said, according to Al Jazeera.

And Nvidia isn’t the only giant in your fund. Seven companies, Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Tesla, made up about 32.5% of the S&P 500 fund on Nov. 19. Most of them have a famous face at the top. When an index of 500 companies leans that hard on a handful of them, it also leans on the handful of people running them.

It’s not just CEOs

The same is true of the people we elect. In April 2025, after the president announced sweeping tariffs, U.S. stocks lost more than $6 trillion in value in two days, NPR reported, citing The Wall Street Journal.

And today, the president said he called into a private company’s board meeting, and that company reversed a decision its own chair had announced the week before.

You can think those calls were right or wrong. Either way, they show how much can rest on a single announcement or a single phone call, and that’s true no matter who is in the White House or which party runs Congress.

What would a rival want?

This is the uncomfortable part. Nvidia’s board says it’s investigating reporting that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” and CBS News reported that the woman at the center of it was suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for China. China denies it, and Huang hasn’t been charged with anything.

We don’t know what that effort was after, and nobody has reported that it was trying to move markets. Usually, the warning from U.S. officials is about stealing secrets. In 2022, then-FBI Director Christopher Wray told business leaders that China wanted to “ransack” Western companies’ intellectual property, and that its spies were going after companies “from Fortune 100s to startups,” Fortune reported. China called those accusations groundless.

But think about it from a rival’s side. If a scandal around one executive can rattle the country’s most important chip company, and with it the retirement savings of millions of Americans, then the person at the top isn’t just a business risk. They’re a national security risk. That isn’t a claim about what happened here. It’s a question about what’s possible, and Nvidia’s board seems to be asking it too. Today it created a new National Security and Export Control Committee.

We watch the faces

Here’s what bugs us. We know these people’s faces. We know Huang’s leather jacket. We know which senator went viral this week and what the president posted. What we pay much less attention to is what they actually do: the board votes, the filings, the bills, the rules.

The numbers back that up. In the Annenberg Public Policy Center’s 2026 civics survey, only 65% of U.S. adults could name all three branches of government, and 16% couldn’t name any, WJLA reported.

Nvidia’s warning about depending on its leaders sat in a public filing anyone could read. Most of us never did. That’s not a knock on anyone. Filings are long and boring, and a scandal is not. But the boring part is where the power actually shows up.

Forward

Concentration isn’t automatically bad. Huang built Nvidia, and today’s jump shows how much investors value him. But a system where one resignation, one post or one phone call can swing your retirement account is more fragile than most of us realize until it shows up on a statement.

Some things that would help: companies naming real succession plans before a crisis, boards that make their own calls and explain them to shareholders, and voters paying as much attention to what officials vote on as to what they post. For the rest of us, it starts with knowing what’s actually inside the funds we own.

So here’s our question: should any one person, a CEO, a senator or a president, have this much sway over your 401(k)? Tell us where you land in the comments.

stories.title: 11 days later, he’s back. Nvidia just rehired Jensen Huang.
stories.dek: Nvidia’s board brought its founder back as CEO this morning, less than two weeks after he resigned amid reports that included a suspected Chinese spy. The stock opened about 30% higher. The investigations are still open.
stories.body:
Eleven days. That’s how long Nvidia, the company that makes the chips nearly every big tech company is lining up to buy, went without the man in the black leather jacket.

This morning, Monday, Nov. 23, Nvidia’s board voted unanimously to bring Jensen Huang back as president and CEO and to put him back on the board, “effective immediately,” according to the company’s filing with the SEC. The stock opened roughly 30% higher, TechCrunch reported.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in the company’s statement. He also said, “I can’t wait to get back to work.”

How we got here

Huang resigned on Nov. 12, and the reporting behind it moved fast. CBS News reported that he had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China, and, citing The New York Times, an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. TechCrunch reported that Huang admitted to at least two extramarital affairs.

What’s confirmed and what isn’t matters here. China has denied the spying claims, CBS reported. Nvidia’s own statement doesn’t confirm or deny them. It refers to “recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort,” which is not the same as saying he helped one. Huang has not been charged with anything.

While he was gone, chief financial officer Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO and kept her finance job too.

“Does not intend to reinstate”

Here’s the part that makes today so strange. On Nvidia’s earnings call last week, board chair Harvey Jones said the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” CBS reported. According to TechCrunch, Nvidia had already hired the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find his replacement.

Outside the boardroom, people did what people do now: they started a petition. It passed 180,000 signatures within days, Al Jazeera reported, and Elon Musk signed it. TechCrunch named other signers, including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

Huang left the door open himself. Last week he said that if the “board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

The president called in

Then the White House got involved. President Trump said he spoke directly to Nvidia’s board, and he told CNBC he was “represented in the board meeting” and that his intervention mattered, Al Jazeera reported. A week earlier, asked about Huang coming back, he had said, “I would not mind seeing that.”

After the announcement, he posted on Truth Social: “The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.” He added, “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Trump also said the attorney general had confirmed there is no evidence Huang did anything illegal, TechCrunch reported. That claim comes from the president. We haven’t seen a Justice Department statement saying it.

The board’s statement makes the same point in its own words. It says it “received input from senior levels of the United States government,” and based on that input it is “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” It doesn’t say which officials, or what they reviewed.

Why Wall Street cared this much

To understand a 30% jump, it helps to know what Nvidia is. Huang co-founded it in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, and the three famously planned the company in a Denny’s in San Jose, according to Nvidia’s history. For years it was the gaming company, the one whose GeForce graphics cards made PC games look the way they do. Then it turned out the same kind of chip was exactly what giant data centers needed to run chatbots and the cloud, and Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies on Earth.

Analyst Dan Ives had warned that Nvidia could lose as much as 30% of its value without him. Today he said “the board knew it had no choice but to bring him back,” and called Nvidia “the linchpin to the global economy.” Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge told CBS that Huang “was a singular CEO” who kept “an extremely flat corporate structure, making him difficult to replace.”

The ripple went well past one stock. Al Jazeera reported the Nasdaq up 6.7% and the S&P 500 up 4.6% in Monday trading. If you own an S&P 500 index fund, in a 401(k) or anywhere else, you own a little Nvidia.

Not everyone is cheering

Lawmakers in both parties pushed back on the decision, Al Jazeera reported. Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote on X, “This reckless decision to bring back Jensen Huang does not change the fact that Huang and NVIDIA still owe Congress answers.”

And there’s a question we kept coming back to around America House today: if Jensen Huang were a woman, would she be back?

We can’t know for sure. Every case is different, and Nvidia’s board says it decided based on Huang’s record and on what U.S. officials told it. But the research on how men and women get punished at work points in one direction.

Economists Mark Egan, Gregor Matvos and Amit Seru studied about 1.2 million U.S. financial advisers. After misconduct, women were 20% more likely than men to lose their jobs and 30% less likely to find a new one, even though men were three times as likely to commit misconduct in the first place, Stanford Graduate School of Business reported.

At the very top, the pattern looks similar. A 2018 study in the Journal of Management looked at CEO departures from 2000 to 2014 and estimated that women CEOs were about 45% more likely to be dismissed than men. The gap was biggest at companies that were doing well, according to Clemson University, whose researchers co-wrote the study.

Nvidia is doing very well. Huang got a petition with 180,000 signatures, a call from the president and his job back in 11 days. Neither study looked at a case like this one, so they can’t tell us what this board would have done with a woman in the same seat. They do show why so many people are asking.

The investigations aren’t over. Al Jazeera reported that probes by the SEC and the Justice Department are still going. Inside Nvidia, a committee of independent directors, working with outside lawyers, is still looking into the foreign intelligence reporting, and the company says that review “will proceed to conclusion.”

The board also added guardrails. There’s a new National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors to watch over trade rules and national security risks, new national security lawyers, and a search for a chief compliance officer who will report to a board committee.

Forward

Two things can be true at once. Huang built one of the most important companies in America, and investors clearly believe it runs better with him in charge. And the questions that pushed him out haven’t been publicly answered yet. The board says Washington signed off. Congress says it still wants answers.

What to watch: whether the SEC or the Justice Department says anything on the record, what Nvidia’s internal review finds, and whether Congress gets the briefing it’s asking for.

So here’s our question: if a woman CEO had faced the same reports, would she have gotten the same second chance? Tell us where you land in the comments.

stories.title: How to Make a Nonpartisan Thanksgiving Table
stories.dek: Greek Maria got me thinking about what a nonpartisan Thanksgiving table would actually taste like. By Sydney Thackray.
stories.body:
This is my first Thanksgiving in the D.C. area. We’re opening the doors at America House for Friendsgiving and inviting the friends we’ve made since we started, people who believe in what we’re building here.

Back home in Los Angeles, just about every dish made a pit stop at Erewhon on the way over. This year I’m excited for a real fall and the kind of Thanksgiving where the whole house smells like dinner before anybody sits down. I can’t wait to see what our new friends bring to the table.

Greek Maria came over to America House for our midterm livestream. She has a bit where she guesses your political party based on what you like to eat. Ice cream flavors, pizza toppings, chips. If she can do that with a bag of chips, what would happen if we gave her the entire Thanksgiving table? (More on Greek Maria’s political guessing game)

I’ll go first. The turkey leans right. My evidence is that half the table will admit it’s dry and then be personally offended if you suggest serving something else next year. It has tradition on its side, and, to be fair, I’d miss it too.

This is where I bring in the pineapple. Yes, the same fruit that can start a fight on a pizza. I put it inside the bird with rosemary and sage, and I work garlic-sage butter under the skin. The pineapple gives the roast a sweet, herbal aroma, and a thermometer helps me pull the turkey before the breast dries out. If your family objects to the pineapple, tell them they can vote after they’ve had a bite.

The turkey: the Republican with a pineapple amendment

For a 12–14 lb turkey. You’ll need 1 fully thawed turkey, 1 stick (½ cup) softened unsalted butter, 4 minced garlic cloves, 2 tablespoons chopped fresh sage, 1 small pineapple, a few sprigs each of rosemary and sage, 1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves, kosher salt and black pepper, 2 halved onions, 2 chopped carrots, 4 more garlic cloves, and 1½–2 cups low-sodium beef broth.

  1. Heat the oven to 325°F. Remove the neck and giblets from the cavities and pat the turkey dry. Mix the softened butter with the minced garlic and chopped sage. Starting at the cavity end, gently slide your fingers between the breast meat and skin. Work the butter under the skin without tearing it.
  2. Cut the top and peel off the pineapple, then cut it into large chunks. Put a few chunks, the rosemary, and the sage sprigs loosely inside the cavity. Season the outside with salt, pepper, thyme, and whatever extra spices you like. Put the onions, carrots, remaining garlic, and broth in the roasting pan. Set the turkey breast-side up on a rack above the broth.
  3. Budget about 3½–4 hours and use an instant-read thermometer to judge doneness. The thickest part of the breast, the innermost thigh and wing, and the center of the largest pineapple chunk in the cavity should all reach 165°F. Keep the thermometer off the bone when checking the meat. The broth can make opening the oven feel like opening a steam room, so stand back when you open the door. Rest the bird for 20–30 minutes, then remove and discard the cavity aromatics before carving. (FoodSafety.gov turkey roasting guide)

Cornbread is a Democrat

My evidence is the following very leftist recipe. Buy a box of Trader Joe’s Cornbread Mix, make it exactly the way the box tells you, and serve it warm. If anybody asks how you made it, hand them the box.

Brussels sprouts are the swing vote

Half the table has been voting against Brussels sprouts since somebody made them finish the boiled ones as a kid. I roast mine cut-side down so the edges get crispy, then give them balsamic and a little honey. Watch the person who said, “Don’t put any on my plate,” start eating them straight off the sheet pan.

Trim 1½ lb Brussels sprouts, peel away any damaged outer leaves, and halve them lengthwise. Toss with 2 tablespoons olive oil, salt, and black pepper. Arrange cut-side down on a sheet pan and roast at 425°F for 20–25 minutes, until browned and tender. Brush with 1 tablespoon balsamic glaze during the last few minutes. Finish with a drizzle of honey and a sprinkle of fresh thyme.

Sweet potatoes are the moderates

Sweet potatoes have one foot in dinner and one foot in dessert. Once I whip in the butter, cream, honey, and cinnamon, they could make a pretty good case for sitting next to the pie. I tear fresh basil over the top to remind them they still have to sit with the vegetables.

Peel and cube 2 lb sweet potatoes. Boil in salted water for 15–20 minutes, until fork-tender, and drain well. Whip with 4 tablespoons butter, ⅓ cup warmed heavy cream, 1 tablespoon honey, and ½ teaspoon cinnamon. Add salt to taste and scatter torn fresh basil over the top just before serving.

Cranberry sauce is the independent

It’s bright red, which might tempt you to call the race early. Give it a minute. The turkey gets a spoonful, the mushroom Wellington gets one, and I’ll happily swipe up what’s left with a dinner roll. I add just enough honey to take the edge off. I still want it to have a little bite.

Bring one 12 oz bag of fresh cranberries, ½ cup water, and 4 tablespoons honey to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer, stirring occasionally, for 10–15 minutes, until most of the berries burst. Mash a few against the side of the pot if you like a smoother sauce. Taste for sweetness, then pour into a bowl, let it cool, and refrigerate. It’ll thicken as it chills.

Mashed potatoes are the bipartisan bill

You can disagree about every other thing on this menu and still agree that I should’ve made more potatoes. The butter and cream do most of the work, but the sour cream is what gets the person who said “I’m stuffed” ten minutes ago to reach for the serving spoon.

Peel and chunk 2½ lb Yukon Gold potatoes. Start them in cold salted water, bring to a boil, and cook for 15–20 minutes, until tender. Drain, then mash with 4 tablespoons butter, ½ cup warmed heavy cream, and ½ cup sour cream. Season with salt and a dash of black pepper.

Mac and cheese is off the political spectrum

Everybody loves mac and cheese. Once it hits the table, the only thing anyone wants to know is who’s getting the corner piece with all the buttery breadcrumbs.

For a 9 × 13-inch baking dish. You’ll need 1 lb elbow macaroni, 6 tablespoons butter (divided), 4 tablespoons all-purpose flour, 4 cups whole milk, 1 cup each of grated sharp yellow cheddar, white cheddar, and Gruyère, ¾ cup breadcrumbs, salt, and black pepper.

  1. Heat the oven to 375°F. Boil the macaroni in salted water until it’s about 1–2 minutes shy of al dente, then drain and put it in a buttered baking dish.
  2. Melt 4 tablespoons butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for about 1 minute to make the roux. Slowly whisk in the milk and cook, stirring, until the sauce thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon. Take it off the heat and stir in the three cheeses a handful at a time until smooth. Season with salt and pepper.
  3. Pour the cheese sauce over the macaroni and stir to coat. Melt the remaining 2 tablespoons butter, toss it with the breadcrumbs, and scatter them over the top. Bake for 20–25 minutes, until the edges bubble and the breadcrumbs are golden.

The mushroom Wellington leans left

The Wellington’s big reform is giving the vegans something of their own to carve. I cook the mushrooms down in red wine with Dijon and thyme, then wrap the whole thing in puff pastry. If I were the turkey, I’d be a little nervous about running for reelection.

For one Wellington. You’ll need 1 sheet vegan puff pastry, thawed according to the package, 2 tablespoons olive oil plus more for brushing, 1 diced yellow onion, 1½ lb finely diced mushrooms, 1 bay leaf, 1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves, 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard, 2 cups dry red wine, 1 tablespoon all-purpose flour, salt, and black pepper. Use a vegan-labeled wine for the vegan version, or use 1 cup vegetable broth and 1 tablespoon balsamic vinegar for an alcohol-free filling.

  1. Sauté the onion in the oil until soft. Add the mushrooms, bay leaf, thyme, salt, and pepper. Cook in a wide skillet until the mushrooms give up their water and start browning. Stir in the mustard and wine and simmer uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the mixture is thick and the pan has no pooled liquid. Remove the bay leaf. Sprinkle in the flour a little at a time, stirring, and cook another 1–2 minutes. Let the filling cool completely.
  2. Unfold the still-cool pastry on a parchment-lined sheet pan. Spoon the filling down the middle, leaving room around the edges. Fold the long sides over the filling, pinch the seam and ends closed, then turn it seam-side down. Keep the pastry thick enough to hold the filling. Brush with olive oil and cut a few shallow vents across the top.
  3. Bake at 400°F for 30–40 minutes, until the pastry is puffed and deep golden. Let it rest 10 minutes before slicing. For the dairy version, fold up to 2 cups grated Gruyère into the cooled filling, divide it between two pastry sheets, and use an egg wash if you like.

To give vegan guests more of the menu, use maple syrup in place of honey, and set aside some of the boiled potatoes from each batch before adding dairy. Mash those portions with plant butter, unsweetened oat cream, and vegan sour cream where called for.

I’m still undecided about the Hawaiian rolls

Give me one warm from the oven with rosemary butter and I’ll probably forget what you asked.

Set 12 Hawaiian rolls on a baking sheet. Douse the tops with 4 tablespoons melted butter and sprinkle with 1 teaspoon each of fresh thyme leaves, chopped sage, and finely chopped rosemary. Bake at 350°F for about 5 minutes, just until warm. Do this right before you call everybody to dinner.

The real test

It’s gotten a little ridiculous how quickly we decide what somebody believes based on what they look like, drive, shop for, or order for dinner. We do it before they’ve even said a word, and pretty soon we’re treating a guess like a fact. I figured I’d take that habit all the way to the Thanksgiving table. If the turkey’s right and the cornbread is a Democrat, what does that tell me about the person who goes back for seconds of both?

If you want to borrow Greek Maria’s game for Thanksgiving, let everybody name the politics of one thing on their plate and make their case. If you ask me, the real test of a nonpartisan table is who comes back to the kitchen the next morning and makes a sandwich with a little of everything.

stories.title: A Creator House With a Purpose: America House Wants You to Help Build a Better Country
stories.dek: Creator houses showed how much attention a group of people under one roof could capture. Dame Sydney Thackray on what America House wants to do with it, and how you can be part of it from anywhere.
stories.body:
Creator houses showed us how much attention a group of people living under one roof could capture. You followed their friendships, watched the drama, learned the dances, and came back for the next video.

But what was everyone building toward?

I’m Dame Sydney Thackray, and that question is at the heart of America House.

We saw the attention surrounding Hype House and the creator houses that followed. They brought people together around personalities and a constant stream of entertainment. The next post gave you another reason to watch. The shared destination was harder to find.

I wanted to take that ability to bring people together and give it a purpose that could last beyond the feed.

At America House, we’re asking you to watch what we’re doing, watch what we’re building, and participate yourself.

Because imagine what that attention could accomplish if even a fraction of the people watching decided to help.

A house where the next idea can become something real

America House is a creator house and a constant builder space in McLean, Virginia. We bring creators and civic technology builders together to work on making America a better place—and make the process something people want to follow.

There are personalities, friendships, disagreements, and the everyday absurdity of living and working together. You get to know the people. You also get to see what they are trying to accomplish.

A conversation about confusing legislation can lead to work on VoteImpact, which helps people understand bills, explore their consequences, and contact their representatives. Questions about where tax dollars go connect to ImpactLine, our work to make government spending easier to understand.

These are projects people can question, contribute to, and help improve.

The house gives that work a place to happen continuously. Someone brings a problem to the table. Someone else knows how to explain it. A builder starts working on a tool. A creator helps people discover it. The audience brings questions and experiences we might otherwise miss.

That is the relationship we want between making content and making progress.

You don’t have to live here to be part of it

The physical house is the starting point for a nationwide movement.

You can take a video of yourself explaining a problem in your town. Build a civic technology project. Gather your community around an issue you want to address. Bring your skills to something another person has started.

Maybe you know how to code. Maybe you know how to get twenty neighbors into a room. Maybe you’re good at asking the question everyone else has been avoiding.

There is room for all of that.

We want people across the country to see America House and recognize something they could start where they live. A gathering around a kitchen table. A local project with a clear goal. A video that helps people understand an issue well enough to get involved.

The movement grows when people take ownership of a piece of it.

A shared purpose without requiring the same opinions

America House is nonpartisan, with four shared pillars: transparency, accountability, participation, and abundance.

We want people to understand how decisions are made, see whether promises lead to results, have a meaningful way to participate, and help build a country where more people can thrive.

There will be disagreements about how to get there. Those disagreements belong in the work. We should be able to question an idea, examine its consequences, and improve it together.

Having a shared purpose gives us a reason to stay at the table.

Something worth coming back to

A video can disappear from your feed in seconds. What it inspires someone to build can last much longer.

That is what I want America House to make possible: a place people follow because they care about the people inside it, and a movement they join because they care about what we could accomplish together.

Watch us. Challenge our ideas. Bring your own.

Then pick something you want to make better, find your people, and start building. That is how America House becomes bigger than a house.

stories.title: GTA VI Is Finally Here. Look What America Did While We Waited.
stories.dek: Thirteen years after GTA V, the return to Vice City tells us how much America has changed and how good the games industry has gotten at keeping us logged in.
stories.body:
“Are we going to get GTA VI, or are we going to get World War III first?” For years, that was the kind of question people asked when the news got weird and Rockstar still hadn’t put out the game. Today, November 19, Rockstar answered the GTA part. Grand Theft Auto VI is out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, 13 years, two months and two days after GTA V arrived. (Rockstar Games · Rockstar’s GTA V release announcement)

From a couple of pixels to a whole city

The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997, when only 18% of U.S. households used the internet. You looked down on tiny cars tearing through blocky versions of American cities. GTA III brought the series into 3D in 2001, and Vice City gave it a neon, 1980s take on Miami a year later. The appeal was simple. You could follow the story, or you could ignore it, steal a car and see where the road went. (The Guardian’s GTA history · U.S. Census Bureau’s historical internet data)

This time, we’re back in a present-day Vice City with Jason and Lucia, whose botched score lands them in the middle of a statewide conspiracy. In the first trailer, vertical videos show the kind of Florida chaos built for a social feed, including a guy trying to get an alligator out of a pool. That December 2023 trailer racked up 90.4 million YouTube views in 24 hours. Then a release planned for 2025 moved to May 2026 and again to November. (Rockstar Games · Ars Technica’s trailer coverage · Guinness World Records · Rockstar’s May 2026 date announcement · Rockstar’s November 2026 date announcement)

What America did before GTA VI

When GTA V came out, the iPhone 5s was still three days away. In May 2013, 56% of American adults owned a smartphone, according to Pew Research Center. In 2026, 91% did. Over roughly the same stretch, the country grew from about 316 million people in 2013 to 341.8 million in 2025. (Apple · Pew Research Center · 2013 Census estimate · 2025 Census estimate)

In those years, the Supreme Court recognized a nationwide right to same-sex marriage. NASA and SpaceX sent astronauts into orbit from American soil for the first time since the shuttle era. COVID-19 sent millions of workers home. Then ChatGPT arrived, and people started handing a chatbot their first drafts. A kid who played GTA V after middle school could be dropping their own kid off at school today. (Obergefell v. Hodges · NASA · U.S. Census Bureau on remote work · OpenAI’s 2022 announcement)

That’s why “we got ___ before GTA VI” worked. When a witness testified about UFOs in Congress in 2023, the internet’s version was, “We got aliens before GTA VI.” The World War III version gave the same joke a darker edge. The news could feel ridiculous and frightening on the same afternoon. For a second, everybody in the comments could agree on one thing. Surely the game would be out by now. (Know Your Meme)

How many copies did GTA sell?

Before GTA VI launched, Take-Two reported more than 475 million units worldwide for the franchise. Rockstar says GTA V alone accounted for nearly 235 million, including 11.21 million in its first 24 hours, according to Guinness World Records. The lifetime figures are publisher sell-in totals, which can include copies shipped to retailers. (Take-Two’s SEC filing · Take-Two’s launch announcement · Guinness World Records)

For GTA VI, analytics firm Sensor Tower estimated about 19.1 million copies sold by Thursday morning, Reuters reported. Take-Two had yet to release an official launch-day count. And in Miami on Wednesday night, the Heat played a Vice City-themed game. The real city was throwing a party for its fictional counterpart. (Reuters)

What all that time online costs

Part of the reason the wait lasted so long in public is that GTA V never really left. Rockstar brought it and GTA Online to newer consoles. Players built roleplay communities, while Rockstar kept earning money from virtual currency and in-game purchases. A game people once finished could become a place they went back to every night. (Rockstar on GTA Online’s rerelease · Rockstar’s roleplay community update · Take-Two’s SEC filing)

There’s real pleasure in that. A game can be where you catch up with a friend who moved away. It can also be where you look up at 2 a.m. and realize you have work in four hours. The World Health Organization recognizes gaming disorder when people lose control over play and keep going despite serious harm to their daily lives. It affects a small share of players. Research has also linked problematic gaming to shorter sleep and worse sleep quality. You can recognize the trade-off long before it gets that serious. What did you mean to do with that evening? (World Health Organization · Systematic review of gaming and sleep)

There’s a physical cost, too. A 2019 study estimated that the electricity used for video gaming in the U.S. was associated with 24 million metric tons of carbon dioxide a year. That was an estimate for gaming as a whole at the time. The study also found that cloud gaming can draw more energy through data centers and networks than playing locally. (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory)

So yes, enjoy Vice City. Get your friends together and see what took Rockstar thirteen years. Then give one of those evenings to the city you actually live in. Go see the friend you only talk to online, or show up for something happening down the street. The game can wait. Ask any GTA fan.

stories.title: A hacking gang says it hit Visa and Chase, and gave them 48 hours. Here’s what’s real.
stories.dek: The gang hasn’t shown any proof. Visa says a vendor was hit, not Visa. Chase says its outage was a software bug. Here’s what to do with your cards anyway.
stories.body:
The claim

A ransomware gang called n0n added Visa and JPMorgan Chase to its leak site this week, first reported by Cybernews on Nov. 17. It set a 48-hour window for negotiations before it says it will publish data it claims to have taken. It hasn’t said what kind of data or how much, and no sample has been reported.

The group was first tracked in mid-September. The week before, it claimed Expedia as a victim.

What Visa says

Visa said it is aware of the claims and that the incident started at a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region. It said its own systems were not involved or affected and that there is no sign payment data, including card numbers, was compromised. Visa hasn’t named the provider.

What Chase says

JPMorgan Chase said a recent service outage was caused by a software bug and that it found no evidence of a cyberattack. It hasn’t said whether anything connects that outage to the gang’s claims. So far the only overlap reported is the timing.

What you can do today

You don’t need to cancel your cards over an unproven claim. Do check your recent transactions, turn on purchase alerts in your bank’s app, and be careful with any email or text about “the Visa breach” that asks you to log in or confirm your card. Scammers follow headlines. Go to your bank’s app or the number on the back of your card instead.

A gang’s leak-site post is not proof, and a company’s statement isn’t the last word either. The 48-hour clock runs out this week. We’ll tell you what, if anything, gets released. Do you check your bank app every day?

stories.title: First the planes. Then the banks. Now the NSA's classified network went down.
stories.dek: The spy agency's internal network failed on Tuesday, capping a week of big outages. Officials say it was maintenance, not hackers. Here's what we know and what we don't.
stories.body:
What happened

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, the National Security Agency's classified internal network stopped working, according to multiple U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News and NBC News. CNN first reported it. It's the network NSA staff use to store and share classified information inside the agency.

At the agency's headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, non-emergency staff were told to come in at staggered times, so thousands of people wouldn't all try to log on at once while the network was struggling. Sources told CBS some work was moved to other NSA sites around the country. The gates and the rest of the campus kept running.

What the NSA says

The agency called it a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" and said its most important missions stayed fully running. Two sources said the trouble came from routine software patching. As of the latest reports, nobody had said how long the network was down or when it would be fully back.

Was it an attack?

Officials say there is no sign of one. Two U.S. officials and a senior U.S. cybersecurity official said they saw no evidence of a cyberattack. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Tuesday that it was not an attack and not a coordinated effort by another country, and pointed to companies and agencies patching their systems.

On Wednesday in Manila, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the problems were "completely unrelated one from another" and that there is "zero evidence" hackers or other bad actors were involved.

Why people are asking

Because it's been that kind of week. Last Thursday, a worldwide Microsoft outage took down Outlook and Teams. On Friday, a nationwide ground stop held every departing flight in the country for hours. Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and U.S. Bank hit disruptions. Apple's services went down too. Then the NSA.

Mass outages this close together are rare. But the explanations so far have a common thread, and it isn't hackers. Federal officials blamed the FAA failure on a contractor doing maintenance updates. Apple's outage was tied to an internal update. The NSA points to scheduled maintenance. Microsoft said its problem was technical, not malicious. Experts note that short outages on government networks are fairly common, often because the software is complex and not always kept up to date.

What we don't know

Why so many large systems failed in the same few days. Officials say the causes are different, and we have seen no evidence that says otherwise. We also don't yet know exactly what went wrong at the NSA, or why a routine update could take down a network that is built with backups.

The scary version is a hidden attack. The likelier version is almost as worrying: the systems we depend on can be knocked over by their own updates. What would help is slower, tested rollouts, real backups, and plain answers from the agencies when something breaks. Coincidence or a pattern? Tell us what you think.
